content: Deciduous teeth, also referred to as milk teeth, baby teeth, temporary teeth, or primary teeth, are the initial set of teeth that develop in humans and many other mammals. These teeth begin forming during the embryonic stage of development and become visible in the mouth, a process known as eruption, during infancy. While they are typically replaced by permanent teeth, in cases where permanent replacements are absent, deciduous teeth can remain functional for many years. The formation of deciduous teeth begins during the embryonic phase of pregnancy, specifically around the sixth week of development, when the dental lamina starts to form. This process initiates at the midline and progresses toward the posterior regions. By the eighth week of embryonic development, ten distinct areas on both the upper and lower arches are established, which will eventually develop into the deciduous dentition. These teeth continue to form until they erupt into the oral cavity. In total, there are twenty deciduous teeth, with five teeth per quadrant and ten per arch. The eruption of these teeth typically begins at around six months of age and continues until the child is approximately twenty-five to thirty-three months old. The first teeth to erupt are usually the mandibular central incisors, while the last to appear are the maxillary second molars. The deciduous dentition consists of central incisors, lateral incisors, canines, first molars, and second molars, with one of each type present in each quadrant, making a total of four of each tooth type. All deciduous teeth are eventually replaced by their permanent counterparts, except for the first and second molars, which are replaced by premolars. Deciduous teeth remain in the mouth until around the age of six, at which point the permanent teeth begin to erupt, resulting in a mixed dentition phase. The eruption of permanent teeth triggers a process called root resorption, where the roots of the deciduous teeth are dissolved and absorbed by the developing permanent teeth. This process, known as exfoliation, typically occurs between the ages of six and twelve. By the age of twelve, most individuals have only permanent teeth remaining. Deciduous teeth play a critical role in the development of the oral cavity. They serve as a guide for the eruption of permanent teeth, as the permanent teeth develop from the same tooth buds as the deciduous teeth. Additionally, the presence of primary teeth is essential for the proper development of the jaw muscles and bones, as well as for maintaining the necessary space for the permanent teeth. Deciduous teeth also contribute to a child’s ability to chew food effectively and develop proper speech patterns. The American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry recommends that infants visit a dentist by the age of six months or shortly after the eruption of the first primary tooth, but no later than the age of one. During this visit, parents can receive guidance on how to care for their child’s deciduous teeth and prevent oral diseases. Parents should avoid cleaning pacifiers with their mouths to prevent the transmission of cavity-causing bacteria, such as Streptococcus mutans, to the child. To further reduce the risk of oral disease, parents should avoid giving sweetened liquids in bottles or sippy cups, except during meal times. Only water or milk should be used in these containers. Additionally, bottles should not be taken to bed with children, as this can lead to the development of cavities, commonly referred to as baby bottle caries. These cavities occur when sweet liquids, such as juice or sweetened milk, pool around the teeth while the child sleeps. Dental researchers emphasize the importance of starting oral hygiene care as soon as the first tooth erupts, which typically occurs around six months of age. Parents can use an infant toothbrush with water to clean the teeth. Once the child reaches the age of two, a small amount of fluoride toothpaste can be introduced to further protect the teeth from decay.
